segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: This side of the following tape was recorded on July 5th, 1973 at the home of Mr. Rudolph Nordby in Genesee, Idaho. The voices on the tape are those of Rudolph Nordby and the interviewer, Rob Moore. That story you told about being dropped off at the farm place in Palouse, pretty interesting to wonder if you could talk about that again.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: When we moved in, when you came in to, when you came by train in T and what happened then? We came in by train into Palouse and then of course we hired a cab with a driver to take it out. This was in February and the road was just breaking up, breaking holes. We'd be going along there and we were supposed to be going along there. We'd be driving, we'd be mingling around in this place. The interesting thing about that was that my grandmother was there and of course she taught nothing like Norwegian. She scolded this fellow with his driving, so I said, that is Genesee's driving. It went on a lot. His name was Genesee.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did he speak Norwegian?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No, he didn't speak Norwegian. She of course had no idea that Norwegian would ever have that here. It was kind of interesting. It was six and a half mile drive.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did he ever say anything back to her? Did he ever tell her that he spoke Norwegian?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah, he did. He talked Norwegian afterwards. Then of course he'd done some terrible things.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How many of you were there?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I were five children and two and a grandmother. Five, eight. And we'd drive half way.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you have all your tools and things along with you? That trip came out?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: We hadn't. They were shipped out soon. Then of course he had to go and get a team and go and get the stuff. That's about a day's drive. Right.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: So you were stranded out on the home place there? Were there buildings up there?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh yeah… there were several buildings there. So we were kind of covered. Of course in those days they could make food out of those things.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Had you brought a bunch of food in with you or did you have to start?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I suspect that we bought some groceries in the police department. It could be my guess. I don't care. I just tried to have to. I'd have to be. We didn't have any relatives that we could sponge out. So I think that is about shadow.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of things did you start doing when you got there to the police?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, about the first thing they did was to try to fix up the house a little, so it was a little more livable. And get organized on that. Well, of course we had to get out and start buying boxes and equipment, which was very mediocre, of course. Most of it was used machine and things were done.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was there land cleared on this place already?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh yeah, the biggest part of it was in the outdoors.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What crops?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, it just meant like wheat. Or oats.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When you came in February, was there a crop of winter over wheat then? You had to start working right away?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I don't remember whether there was any more winter wheat out there. I rather suspect maybe that everything went into spring crops.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, you were 11 then, right?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of job did you have to do? What did the mill have there?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, it would be milking cows, maybe herding them out there, or they were not very close to the fence. We just had to do whatever was to be done.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was herding cows an all day job?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, if the pasture was good, of course we could bring them in, leave them around and turn them back out.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: I guess it was still pretty wild that there wasn't then?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh yeah, it was a little wild. There were very few church people in there. Of course, we had come from an area where the church was number one, of course, with the folks. That's one reason that mother was discontented, living under those conditions. So then they made a trip down to two jettison and they had a mother and a brother that was living there. Oh, about three miles from the jettison, went to see him. Then they got to looking around, they're like this open country, so I looked for like five or ten different. So they had a chance to buy this 328-pound.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How much did the farms offer?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: ..… but it took many years to get it into producing. The first spring, they said there's a lot of wheat. 180, they considered the whole thing spring wheat. And the quality couldn't see any wheat at all. Why won't you see that? Because that's the money. So they had to cut the whole thing away. And that had sold for six dollars a ton. And it was getting rich very fast.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you remember the move down?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: From Palouse? Oh, yeah. That was quite interesting, too, which was in February, of course. Part of the way it was a pretty good sling. And part of the way it was maybe one little bit on track. I think from Moscow this way and going north, too. So we started out before daylight from up there, a 30-mile drive. And we got in to one of the neighbors up here at Lake Way After Dark. And we kids were riding in the hack. And of course we were just so tired out, we couldn't get it. And then every time we got to a big hill, why? Dad said, you've got to get up. You've got to get up and walk a little easier on the team. And he wanted to keep us awake. So we went to sleep. Well, that just got him excited. Of course, he wanted to get up.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How many trips down did you have to make?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, that I don't remember because we had to give him a little too much. And some of it, of course, had to wait until the roads got through. So we could use a wagon to come.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: So then you moved on to this place here now. And there was a house here then?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, yes. In the Sunbelt, an old-time house that had been used, a portion of it was used in a grocery store. And the counter, or bench, that they used was still here. They had set it outside of the house so they could use a whole room. And then this barn out there was built in, it had been built 27 years when he came here. 27 years old. So that would be in about 75, a little bit. Mr. Trade knew all about it. He was a nearby tourist doctor.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, this place that was the old store here, that the counter was out of? Was that the counter that they bought stuff over? Was it also like a serving counter?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah, they had all the addresses just to come here. They were set the stuff on. It wasn't like an eating counter. Because you said the place was also a stage stuff. Well, they, of course, I suppose, had to have plenty in the house.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long did the stage stuff here? How long was the stage stuff?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I'm not sure about that at first.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did it stop before you came?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, yeah. It didn't go in younger, but sometime old biggest, Warren, was the driver. And it literally was, of course, going down very well. He was a very super.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of goods did the store sell?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, it probably had glass bottles, a little gingham in the middle, and then food.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was it a basic general version of that? The people who owned the place before you, were they still operating the store? Or had the store stopped operation?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No, it didn't start. It didn't start the time.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The post office was no longer there.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I think at that time they had built up the big old town. East of where it is now. So that's where it was.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The picture of your father with the five deer that you killed? I wonder if you had ever gone hunting with your father.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No, I never did. We usually had to. We had to be around to take care of the livestock and stuff. I didn't have much interest in the people that I went with. Sometimes they'd go and come back and look at nothing. But I can recall it. My dad had a big heavy skin line coat. She went and got to the door and then brought her back with her pants. We were just about to stick with my feet.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: They were wool pants?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: He'd get up in a tree and lay it on top of a limb. Maybe for four or five hours waiting for the deer to come out to eat. He'd just try not to move the limb at all.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That was in the wintertime?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, yes. The season, of course, was in the winter. They couldn't have kept it in the region of the public. They got some pretty good information. They always took a lot of cheesecloth. They bought the store and then taken wipes and all the lot of the wipe between. They found the meat could keep so much better.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: He was mostly kept just by the cold?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yes, that's all they had.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: They didn't try smoking either.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: But for the most part, they were in good condition. Sometimes they'd have to drink some of it to walk down. They'd have things to wrap it up and give it to hang up. The lights would come in and cover it with some of the meat at the daytime. And then, of course, if the weather was too warm, they'd understand. Sometimes they'd be pretending before they cooked that out.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When they brought the meat back down, how would they keep it then? They'd keep it the same way, the cold?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, they used to catch, cook it, but they'd jump. They'd take it out of the water and put it out there. They'd drive big spikes in the lot of cheesecloth and hanging up there… a roaster… chips cut off, and then the rain cut off, and then it stood about so much of that, too, because it had to turn warm and not have to drive a can. They'd put it in a can and get greasy, absorbed carbon on the meat. That wasn't exposed to the air.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long did you live in that old, the older house, before you built this place?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I think it was about two years before we built this.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long did this one take to build?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, that took two, three months. The same neighborhood. Mr. Tweed lived the house, and then we had helpers, of course. All along, there was hope in the back of Troy, about four or five miles, and Johnson and all that. That was two days' break. We'd sometimes get out back as far as the spring down this side of Cornwall, up in the up. We'll do something for the place now. There, the team was holding lumber. It was a day night, both of which had two particles. I'd seen a time when you couldn't find a place there in the quarter of a mile.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Really?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I'd found it, filled with my thoughts. This one had an old sister pump that everybody could help themselves.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was the fella's name? That was up there?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, I'll go to the church.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you use to drive back and forth the lumber wagon up to the other side?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: All of the rough ...

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were you driving by yourself in design? How old were you then?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I didn't. I didn't get to do that. I was, oh, fifteen, fifteen to eighteen. One time I went back in there to get a little post. I had six horses and two angles, treads. I felt like I was a pretty good driver… i got back,… and I knew that it looked like it was going to storm. So I got up at three o'clock in the morning. I got a horse and a helmet and started up. One time I got on this side of Cornwall. It was down there, the side of Cornwall. I went to Cornwall and loading press. It started to smoke. I started not letting out. The horses, of course, couldn't hold it. I kept on the brakes. I thought she was going to be in trouble, running over the horses. They all stayed on my feet. Then I came out of the edge grate. I went out and pulled up around the curb. It was kind of simple. I kept the horses and turned one angle to two. I tried my own slip off. So the rack and post, I think I had something like two, twenty post.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I didn't dare to drive any further. I unloaded the other. Then the next day I went and drove down in Mansfield and got on the lower side of it. I had somebody with me so that we could put that on the rack. So that's some of a good experience.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: By the time you were fifteen or so, pretty much taking a man's job in the morning around here? What would a typical day be like?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, we'd get up for a breakfast at six o'clock.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: A big breakfast?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh yeah. In the evening we'd probably come in depending on how we were rushed. Because if we were going to rush we probably wouldn't quit until seven or seven o'clock. So we didn't get up and do a scumbag.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were there thrashing teams that came around here at that time?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh yeah… some other people from up around Detroit followed that. They came in here. And as high as ten bubble teams, two of them, two of them, for making cheese. And I can recall one time holding on my brother's field. They had a big job there. I think thirty stacks of bundles were stacked up. In the folding land they thrashed long enough to get them. The field opened up and then started to rain. It rained for two weeks. And of course we had to feed all those horses all this time. So that tried to cut into the pot.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: It didn't ruin the wheat though?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No, it was in bundles. We dried out. We'd have to walk around of course and if there was some down bundles we'd have to pick them up. Set them up straight so the air would get to them.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What job did you do when the thrashers...?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh I drove one the way.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How did the thrashes work? ... What did they do? How did the machinery work and how did the men work?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well the L machines of course had a long feeder on it. For a while they had the sharp feeder and they were pitching it and they had two men cutting bundles. One man feeding it into a mouth or something. Talked about a dirty job. They sure had it. How they could stand it. So much trouble with smut at that time. You just couldn't hardly see those folks. And how they could stand it. And they had an arctic trigger. They just had it up to a hill and they had it all in one. Of course we were away from the sludge.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When the grain came out of the thrasher was there another wagon waiting there to receive it?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No they stack it out on it. In sacks. Part of it, part of it. About that. Pushing it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: About how many days would it usually take to thrash, say something like your brother's job, a big job like that?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I imagine it took three or four days for the best to get over.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The thrashing machine and crew was rented?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: They owned the machine. And then we hired them. They owned so much. They charged 10, 12, or 15 cents a bushel. And then they would figure out a sack would be two bushels or maybe two and a half. Depending on how much trash there was. Good thing we went to it. One hundred and thirty-five, one hundred and forty cents a sack. Which would be two and a half, for sure.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was this price of the bushel in addition to room and board or did they pay you then to the room and board?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No. Of course after they got that big enough, they had cook wagons. They had cook wagons and cook cooks in there. So they, of course, would have everything ready for the bushel do. They had those bigger outfits, of course, they couldn't keep them out.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: But how many men would there be in one of the bigger outfits?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I think between 20 and 30 men. There would be a kitchen for every two wagons. You have ten wagons, there would be ten drivers. And there would be five or six pitchers. And then you'd have two sack drawers and a sack jig. And a clean-up miller, I'm assuming. And a water holler. A water pulley engine.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Plus the man who was loading, who was beating the wheat?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah, towards last, of course, they had extended pagers and they could just toss a cut in there. And that cut the bubbles through. So the mattress was draining and then got away from there.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That was in your bigger belt or something?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah… they had to come by and find a way to carry it into the kitchen. But when there were smaller crews coming around, it would be that the farm wife would have to prepare all the meals for them. And all that stuff. Of course, the neighbors would get to the avenue. You come and help me and the other crew would help me. So they could attend. They were very much different than what they were. People were turning sound. They were just associative about things like that. They just don't get to the avenue. Unless somebody happens to get injured or something. Get behind you this time or that. They were running a turkey extra combine. Took it off.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How was the threshing season worked? How was it determined who got the machine first and what order people worked?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: The man that was wide awake, of course, he'd engage. You can transfer me if you come when I'm ready for you. If you had a good job, that is just about all. We were a little bit big issue. Couldn't help but think about ourselves.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: About how long would the whole season go on? Who the different farmers would be?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Going around helping each other out. Well, they used to figure hard to 30 to 40 days. That would be done in 10 days. They would try.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: This cooperation that the different farmers would give each other on the farm, you said that when we built this house here, a lot of, what is it, Mr. Tweed came over and helped. Did more neighbors come help then? Were you being prevented?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, that was a little different, of course. Some of the simple work, they could do that. Most of everything is a little complicated, unless you're used to doing a little carton to the left. You'd be in the way of a carton. You wouldn't stand a torch. I won't fix that. Was Mr. Tweed a carpenter? They charge two and a half dollars a day. And you worked in early morning, away from the kitchen. She went just a ton of work in the morning.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you work with a pretty big crew?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, no… probably three men. Two men. Of course. That happened here. We boys did what we got. We cleaned up the trash tank. It's short. Just a little bit. So, when you were about 15, you took over... You started taking a man's portion of work around here. Yeah, pretty much.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You did a lot of plowing ... and growing.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I was ... Usually drove a nine-guard.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How many teams would you have driving a binder?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: One of the teams. Well, we never had one binder to each car. Some of them with a larger car, of course, did. Then, of course, we got into a first binder, and they were a 12-foot cut. And then you got twice as much as a pole binder. You could race as much higher, you wouldn't have to put all that strong. Sometimes that strong goes through the left one. Not just quite a lot of other things.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How many horses did it take to pull one of those big first binders?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Six horses… somewhere I've got a picture of that too, to bring up. I'll try to get some of those things. And I know after a while, someday that I'm not too busy, to see if I can get out, or get in or something. So it'll make it a little easier. But I think that I wouldn't have much to do in the first policy. I don't think that. I've got my daughter, she's down here now. They just came back from there. They came back and she said, yeah. And it'll make them a little too... Every 10 days. Why doesn't he do it for a couple of years? And..., since he's done the cooking.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You were telling me before that when you had your first couple children,… you had them here at this house. And you brought a midwife then.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How did that work? How did you feel about that?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I wasn't much else. We didn't know much choice. We just had to think.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was the midwife? How did you do?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, of course I had a sister too. But you didn't know much.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: I'd like to hear some more about the farming techniques you used and the kind of equipment you used. And when you were quite young, you were still a horse farmer.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, of course we... As soon as the tractors came in, we started to try to accumulate a little bit of oil because we saw that. The difference, it's much different. And I think the first thing I had was a horse that I could plow with and I couldn't see it. And that had steel wheels on it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When was that?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, I don't know. I can't... I'd have to be able to think about that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was that in the 20s or later than that?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: I'd have been in the 20s.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When you were farming with horses, about how long would it take you to plow and create a day already for a person?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, it depended a lot on the weather, of course. It was a real hospital. You had to rest some more so it turned out. But with... I finally got a three-bottle of plow, 12s, three-bottles. But I used eight horses now. And I could plow all six, seven acres a day. Of course, unfortunately, plowed twice a day.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Is that the kind of plow we used to call a foot burner?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah, that's a foot burner… yeah, that's okay… the year we started up here, we had three foot burners. I was, of course, pretty small. And I had the smallest of plow. I had 14 of them. And when I'd get to the corner, I'd put the beam on top of the handle on top of my shoulder so I could drag it out. A lot of people thought that it worked. I enjoyed it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, when you first came, how many acres were you cultivating then? Because you had three plows.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, we were. It was all under cultivation, all that we waste along the creek. Of course, we used to have quite a bit of ground in hay, so we would have to plow it. So I had to... It's been quite materials to go through.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you also harrow at that time?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of a harrow did you use?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, we usually had three sections of harrow. And we got four, so we would sit down and pick out the plow. And I have to go and see that. You could come and cut it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did that harrow look like? How was it shaped?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, it's five bars. I've been to one. And then the times are about so far apart. And the ... Yeah. And then you have a lake. You can set it to steep or you can slope.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And there are how many sections of those bars?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Five bars.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: It was all in a big square shape for a way?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah, just about a square.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How about seed drills and stuff like that? Did you use that one? Seed drill?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, yes… the drill was something that they had, of course, for the rear. I don't remember seeding in any other way here. They had a little shotgun. They had a little outfit set on the back end of the wagon. They had a little weight above the other men. He was men. The way it was turned this way. They had cotton on them. It turned this thing. It would shoot it up with body feet outside.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: It just scattered and didn't cover over anything.

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No, never had to hurt it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: So you grew up in this place here from when you were about 11?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah. And on this place.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And you went to primary school here? What was that? What was it like?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, they had a good school. They had teachers.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did you do when you were already working so hard when you were so young there? When did you have time to go to school?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, of course, there were short turns at that time.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How short?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well, when we were back in Iowa when I was a kid, they had two months in the fall, two months in the spring, and then sometimes summer school. Because everybody had to work. And the winter didn't. It was winter. But here, it's winter here. So we had to go to school.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was it a one-room school?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: No, not here, of course it was.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was it reading?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Yeah, I had it. I had it at school. That was the one that had two grades together. First and second grade. Fifth and sixth, seventh grade. And the high school.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How big a town was Genesee?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, between eight and nine hundred. I was thinking, well, could we go in and out? And I said, well, we got quite a few people, no danger of a massacre last year. And they're still doing it. They like our water… some places.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you have to walk to school?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Oh, yeah… hand-drawn. I don't know. I don't know about the snow. I was just too bad. Especially when the water got high. Father and teacher. I jumped to the right, you know, the hand. Take a seat and walk. But many a time we came home from school and we'd just have to follow the hills. And I couldn't, I couldn't walk across this fact. And I just did it. I just remember I didn't understand why I had to walk.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How far was it to walk?

segments.speaker: Rudolph Nordby
segments.words: Well.
